transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-02
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Ava Martinez, Samir Patel, Lena Cho (Redwood); Brian Thompson, Maya Rios, Kevin Liu (FinEdge)
Links shared: internal pilot runbook (https://redwood.internal/pilot-runbook) - note: redwood link is abbreviated in call, security packet (link shared after)

[00:00] Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check on time — we have 45 minutes on the calendar. Main goals: blockers on networking, review the latest perf numbers Samir ran, and confirm next steps for the security deep dive.

[00:18] Brian (FinEdge): Yep, sounds good. We had a couple things come up this week — primarily on the VPC peering and a weird route thing where the control plane couldn't reach the private workers.

[00:30] Samir (Redwood SE): Right, I jumped into the logs yesterday. Seems like the cross-account route was missing a propagated route from the transit gw, so traffic to the private control plane IPs was dropping. I have a capture in the perf logs, I'll share after.

[00:48] Maya (FinEdge SecOps): To add, our security team saw some source/dest check failures on the NAT gw and we temporarily had to put the worker subnets behind a proxy. That masked things but we want a cleaner fix.

[01:05] Ava: Ok good, that's the networking item. Samir, did you validate security groups and NACLs also? Sometimes the SGs get stuck on the peering side.

[01:20] Samir: I did a quick sweep — SGs look permissive for the control plane ports we listed, but there was a missing explicit route for the pod ENIs. Essentially the V-P-C peering route was not propagating to the route table for workers. I have a screenshot of the route tables I can share.

[01:38] Kevin (FinEdge ML): On the ML side, we ran the baseline inference tests against the hosted API last week and then the private pilot. Latency was generally higher in the pilot, pointing to network overhead and also our initial runtime config — we were on runtime 1.4.8 which doesn't have the new kernel selection heuristics.

[01:58] Samir: Exactly. We re-ran one config with runtime 1.5.2 on a single pool and saw a 12-15% improvement on 1k token generation due to better kernel dispatch and attention fused kernels — though the KV-cache warm path still needs tuning.

[02:18] Brian: Can you explain KV-cache warm path? We keep seeing variable tail latency after a warmup period.

[02:28] Samir: Sure — K-V cache (sometimes transcribed as K-V cash, sorry) is the prefix cache for ongoing chat sessions. If the cache hits are partial because of sequence alignment or different key eviction policies, you get tail spikes. We recommended increasing per-worker cache size and switching to LRU eviction for this workload.

[02:50] Maya: Any security concerns with increasing cache size? Would that change data retention rules or introduce sensitive token persistence?

[03:00] Samir: Good call. The cache in Redwood Private is in-memory on the worker; by default it's ephemeral and not persisted to disk. On the security side, it's covered by the same in-transit encryption; but if you want stronger controls we can enable per-tenant zeroization hooks on shutdown. That ties into KMS/HSM key lifecycle — which we should discuss in the security deep dive.

[03:25] Ava: Let's flag that as an item for SecOps. Maya, do you have specific KMS/HSM constraints?

[03:33] Maya: We need to confirm if Redwood supports external HSMs for key material. Our compliance team prefers HSM-backed keys for production. Right now pilot can use AWS KMS, but product needs to support HSM or bring-your-own-KMS for later.

[03:50] Samir: Redwood Private supports KMS integrations; HSM support is in the roadmap but we do have an HSM bridge option for enterprise customers. I'll put a note and we can bring in the infra security engineer next week.

[04:05] Kevin: Back to perf — what about batching and continuous batching? The pilot tests had relatively low qps per worker so batching didn't trigger aggressively. Any tuning suggestions?

[04:20] Samir: For low QPS you can tune the batching window to be slightly longer (we've seen 10-20ms windows increase token throughput with minimal latency impact for your SLA). Also try adaptive batching: we have policies that increase batch thresholds during off-peak. I can provide config snippets.

[04:42] Brian: We care about 95th percentile latency under 350ms for 512-token prompts. How close are we?

[04:52] Samir: On hosted baseline we were ~220ms at p95. Private pilot on current 1.4.8 config was ~420ms p95. Upgrading to 1.5.2 and enabling the KV cache LRU + small batching window got us down to ~310-330ms p95 on a single-node pilot run. Full cluster results vary, we need the longer seq KV benchmarks to be confident.

[05:18] Ava: Good, that gives us a path. Any regressions on cost with these changes?

[05:25] Samir: Slight increase because larger cache increases memory footprint, and runtime 1.5.2 uses some optimized kernels that are slightly more memory hungry but substantially faster. Overall tokens-per-dollar improved because throughput went up. We should show the delta in the next cost sheet I send.

[05:45] Maya: On networking, we need explicit steps to get peering stable. Brian, are you able to open the VPC peering request and share route table IDs?

[05:53] Brian: Yes, I'll do that today and share in the thread. I think the missing propagation came from the transit gateway config. I'll also pull NAT gateway logs for the window Samir asked about.

[06:05] Samir: Great, please include the ENI IDs too if possible. That helps us map which worker instance had the overflow.

[06:18] Ava: On security docs, I'll send the standard packet and our SOC2 docs, and we'll schedule a security deep-dive next week — likely the week of Sept 13th.

[06:30] Kevin: One more ML item — quantization profile. We tested int8 dynamic and saw a small drop in quality for one evaluation set. Any recommendations?

[06:40] Samir: If quality is slightly impacted, suggest mixed-precision pathing: keep attention and MLP in float16, quantize embeddings and some FF layers. We have a quantization profile guide; I'll attach the example JSON in the follow-up. If you want, we can run a targeted eval on your prompt set.

[06:58] Brian: That would be valuable. We need to be sure no regressions for our top-20 prompts.

[07:05] Ava: We'll run a regression eval set on the top-20 prompts after Samir publishes the config. Samir, can you run the targeted eval with the new runtime and send the report?

[07:15] Samir: Yep, I'll run the eval and include token-level latency and quality delta. Expect it with the KV-cache benchmark.

[07:25] Speaker 6: (unintelligible)

[07:33] Lena (Redwood CSM): Quick note on pilot success criteria — summary from last time: p95 < 350ms, stable throughput for 12h, and security sign-off. Anything to add?

[07:44] Brian: Add: no network-level packet drops >0.1% over a 24h window and encryption keys managed within our KMS/HSM guardrails.

[07:55] Ava: Perfect. We'll capture that in the SOW and pilot checklist.

[08:03] Maya: On the control plane reachability — is there a fallback if peering is delayed? We had some ideas about a NATed egress or reverse-tunneled control plane in emergencies.

[08:14] Samir: We support a fallback where worker pools egress via a customer-managed proxy to the control plane; it's less ideal but works for onboarding. For production we recommend fixing peering or the transit GW config.

[08:30] Brian: Ok we'll prioritize route table propagation.

[08:36] Ava: Next steps recap: Samir to run KV-cache long-seq benchmarks and targeted eval; Brian to share VPC route tables and NAT logs; Maya to confirm KMS/HSM requirements; Ava to send pricing/SOW and security packet. Schedule security deep-dive week of 9/13.

[08:58] Kevin: One tiny thing — can you share the exact kernel flags you used for 1.5.2 test? We want to reproduce.

[09:05] Samir: I'll include the kernel flags and the runtime config in the follow-up. Probably the flags were --kernel-heuristic=auto --attention-fuse=1 and the quant profile we discussed.

[09:18] Ava: Great. Anything else?

[09:22] Brian: No, that's it from me. Thanks.

[09:27] Maya: Thanks all.

[09:30] Ava: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in the thread with artifacts.

[09:35] Meeting end.

Notes: transcript has minor transcription artifacts (names, acronyms sometimes mis-heard). Shared artifacts promised: perf logs (samir/perf.log), KV-cache benchmark CSV, SOW draft, security packet, quantization profile example JSON.
